questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presented with a seizure, having had well-controlled epilepsy for several years on levetiracetam. He had been diagnosed with an Escherichia coli urinary tract infection 1 week earlier for which he was started on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX). He had also started empiric treatment of Mycobacterium abscessus with imipenem–cilastatin, cefoxitin, and amikacin 2 weeks ago.
questions.lead_in: What medication is most likely to have precipitated his new seizure activity?
questions.explanation: Imipenem–cilastatin Imipenem–cilastatin is most likely to be the cause of his seizures. Within the carbapenem drug class, imipenem–cilastatin has been reported to have the highest risk of causing seizures. The other medications listed had reported no risk or minimal risk of causing seizures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q6

questions.question: Interpret the resistance mechanism from the antibiogram pattern.

parts.text: An isolate is resistant to imipenem and meropenem but susceptible to piperacillin and ceftazidime. What is the mechanism of resistance?
An isolate is resistant to ampicillin, cefazolin, and cefoxitin but intermediate to ceftriaxone. What is the mechanism of resistance?

parts_raw.text: Resistant to imipenem and meropenem but sensitive to piperacillin and ceftazidime. What is the mechanism of resistance?
Resistant to amp, cefazolin, and cefox but Intermediate to Ceftriaxone. What is the mechanism of resistance?

questions.model_answer:
a) Carbapenem resistance with retained activity of anti-pseudomonal penicillins/cephalosporins points to a non-enzymatic, carbapenem-selective mechanism: loss of the OprD (D2) porin channel, which carbapenems require for entry, typically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (often combined with basal AmpC). A true carbapenemase would usually also compromise piperacillin and ceftazidime.
b) Resistance to ampicillin, cefazolin AND cefoxitin (a cephamycin) with only intermediate ceftriaxone is the signature of an AmpC beta-lactamase (chromosomal/inducible or plasmid-mediated). AmpC hydrolyzes cephamycins and is not inhibited by clavulanate, distinguishing it from an ESBL (ESBLs spare cefoxitin).

questions.question: For the following antibiotics, describe their (i) capacity for inducing AmpC (strong/weak), (ii) susceptibility to hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), and (iii) whether they are recommended for invasive infection.
questions.question_raw: For the following antibiotics, describe their i) capacity for inducing AmpC (strong/weak), ii) susceptibility to hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), iii) whether they are recommended for invasive infection.

parts.text: Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam
Imipenem

parts_raw.text: Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam
Imipenem

questions.model_answer: a) Ceftriaxone: (i) weak inducer; (ii) high susceptibility to AmpC hydrolysis; (iii) not recommended for invasive infection by an AmpC producer (derepressed mutants emerge on therapy). b) Cefepime: (i) weak inducer; (ii) low susceptibility (zwitterion penetrates rapidly and is less susceptible to AmpC inactivation); (iii) yes — treatment of choice for serious AmpC inducible-resistant strains. c) Piperacillin-tazobactam: (i) weak inducer; (ii) high (tazobactam does not reliably inhibit AmpC, so the penicillin is hydrolysed); (iii) not recommended for invasive AmpC infection. d) Ceftazidime-avibactam: (i) weak inducer; (ii) low (avibactam inhibits class C/AmpC, restoring activity); (iii) yes — recommended for invasive AmpC producers. e) Imipenem: (i) strong inducer; (ii) low (stable to AmpC hydrolysis); (iii) yes — recommended for invasive AmpC infection.
questions.beyond_mandell: The strong/weak induction hierarchy and the pip-tazo/imipenem entries rest on standard AmpC teaching (e.g. Tamma et al., IDSA AmpC guidance); Mandell explicitly supports only that cefepime is less susceptible to AmpC and is treatment of choice for AmpC strains, and that ceftazidime-avibactam's avibactam inhibits class C enzymes.

questions.question: Ertapenem.

parts.text: Antimicrobial class
Coverage
Side effects
What are two advantages and two disadvantages of this antibiotic?

parts_raw.text: a) Antimicrobial class
b) Coverage
c) Side effects
d) What are two advantages and disadvantages of this abx?

questions.model_answer:
a) Carbapenem (beta-lactam).
b) Gram-positive: MSSA, streptococci including Streptococcus pneumoniae; NOT MRSA, coagulase-negative staphylococci, or enterococci. Gram-negative: most Enterobacterales including ESBL- and AmpC-producers; NOT Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter, or Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. Anaerobes: good coverage (including Bacteroides fragilis). No atypical coverage.
c) Common: diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, headache, rash, infusion-site phlebitis. Class effect: lowered seizure threshold (GABA-A antagonism), higher with renal impairment or CNS disease though lower than imipenem; reduces valproic acid levels risking breakthrough seizures. Cross-reactivity in severe penicillin allergy (low).
d) Advantages: (1) Once-daily dosing enabling outpatient/OPAT therapy. (2) Reliable coverage of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales and polymicrobial intra-abdominal infection while sparing anti-pseudomonal carbapenems (stewardship). Disadvantages: (1) No activity against Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, or enterococci. (2) IV only (no oral form) and poor CNS penetration.

cohort_answer.text: a) Carbapenem. b) Gram positive: weaker than other carbapenems, covers MSSA, S. pneumoniae, EXCEPT MRSA/CoNS/enterococcus. Gram negative: most Enterobacteriaceae (incl ESBL/AmpC) EXCEPT Pseudomonas, Stenotrophomonas, B. cepacia, Acinetobacter. Anaerobes: good coverage. No atypical coverage. Ceftriaxone-resistant N. gonorrhoeae remains susceptible. c) Common: diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash, headache, phlebitis. All carbapenems associated with seizures (structural similarity to GABA); higher risk with renal failure/neurologic comorbidities; higher risk with imipenem (1-2%) vs ertapenem (0.1-0.3%); beware valproic acid combination causing subtherapeutic levels. d) Advantages: strong evidence for intra-abdominal infections, ESBL coverage; safe, less epileptogenic than imipenem; once-daily dosing; narrower spectrum aids stewardship. Disadvantages: poor activity vs Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter/enterococcus, no PO option, no CNS penetration, cost.

questions.question: Compare imipenem, meropenem, and ertapenem in terms of coverage for Enterococcus, Stenotrophomonas, Acinetobacter, and Pseudomonas.

Stenotrophomonas maltophilia: none active (intrinsic MBL). Acinetobacter baumannii: imipenem yes, meropenem yes, ertapenem no. Pseudomonas aeruginosa: imipenem yes, meropenem yes, ertapenem no.

cohort_answer.text: Enterococcus (none active vs E. faecium): Imipenem Yes (amp-S E. faecalis), Meropenem Yes (less so than imipenem), Ertapenem No. Stenotrophomonas: all No. Acinetobacter: Imipenem Yes, Meropenem Yes, Ertapenem No. Pseudomonas: Imipenem Yes, Meropenem Yes, Ertapenem No.

questions.question: Name four reasons to add ertapenem to a hospital formulary.
questions.question_raw: Q12 (2007). Name 4 reasons to add Ertapenem to formulary

parts.text: Name four reasons.

parts_raw.text: Name 4 reasons

questions.model_answer: (1) Efficacy: reliable coverage of ESBL/AmpC-producing Enterobacterales and polymicrobial intra-abdominal and complicated skin/soft-tissue infections with strong trial evidence. (2) Convenience: once-daily dosing facilitates outpatient parenteral therapy and simplifies polymicrobial regimens. (3) Safety: comparable to other beta-lactams and less epileptogenic than imipenem. (4) Stewardship: narrower spectrum (no Pseudomonas activity) spares anti-pseudomonal carbapenems and reduces selection pressure.

cohort_answer.text: Efficacy: strong evidence for intra-abdominal infections, ESBL/anaerobe coverage with limited gram positives. Safety: comparable to other beta-lactams, less epileptogenic than imipenem. Quality: once daily dosing facilitates outpatient therapy, simplifies polymicrobial regimens. Stewardship: narrower spectrum than other carbapenems.

questions.question: A multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacillus produces a carbapenemase that is inhibited by EDTA.
questions.question_raw: MDR GNB with carbepenemase inhibited by EDTA.

parts.text: What is the class of carbapenemase?
In what other organism has it been identified?
What are two non-carbapenemase mechanisms of resistance?

parts_raw.text: A.  What is the class?
B.  What other organism has it been identified in?
C.  What are two non-carbepenemase resistance mechanisms?

questions.model_answer:
a) Metallo-beta-lactamase (Ambler class B). These are zinc-dependent enzymes, hence inhibition by the zinc chelator EDTA; examples include IMP, VIM, and NDM-1.
b) Beyond Enterobacterales (e.g. Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli), metallo-beta-lactamases are found in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii (also Serratia, and environmental Stenotrophomonas maltophilia carries an intrinsic MBL, L1).
c) (1) Porin loss/reduced outer-membrane permeability (e.g. loss of OprD in Pseudomonas) limiting drug entry. (2) Upregulation of efflux pumps actively extruding the drug. (A further non-carbapenemase mechanism is PBP target-site alteration.)

cohort_answer.text:
Metallo beta lactamase
Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter baumanii, Enterobacteriaceae, Serratia
Efflux pumps; Target site alteration (changes to PBP); Porin changes

questions.question: A returning patient has a post-fracture wound growing an Acinetobacter resistant to essentially all antibiotics.
questions.question_raw: Returning patient with an Acinetobacter resistant to everything in a post fracture wound.

parts.text: Indicate two mechanisms of resistance to carbapenems.
Give two alternatives for antibiotic treatment.

parts_raw.text: Indicate two mechanisms of resistance to carbapenems
Give two alternatives for antibiotic treatment

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Carbapenem-hydrolyzing enzymes: Ambler class D oxacillinases (intrinsic OXA-51-like and acquired OXA subclasses on chromosome/plasmids) and class B metallo-beta-lactamases (IMP, VIM, NDM). (2) Efflux pumps of the RND family (predominantly AdeABC) which expel beta-lactams and carbapenems; reduced outer membrane permeability via loss/alteration of the OmpAab porin also contributes.
b) (1) Sulbactam (alone or as ampicillin-sulbactam), the most active beta-lactamase inhibitor against Acinetobacter, at >=4 g/day. (2) A polymyxin (colistin or polymyxin B); tigecycline is an additional option.

cohort_answer.text:
Two mechanisms of resistance: Carbapenemase production; Efflux pump; Change in PBPs
Two alternatives: Colistin; Tigecycline

questions.model_answer: 1) Fluconazole over caspofungin (fluconazole achieves high urinary/renal and CSF levels; echinocandins have negligible urinary penetration). 2) Doxycycline over TMP-SMX (doxycycline is not used to treat CDI and carries low risk of inducing CDI). 3) Valganciclovir over valacyclovir (valganciclovir/ganciclovir has potent anti-CMV activity; valacyclovir is poorly active against CMV). 4) Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem (carbapenems interact with anti-epileptics, lowering levels, so the non-carbapenem beta-lactam is preferred). 5) Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (per exam key, for a CNS bacterial infection; ampicillin over cloxacillin is also defensible for Listeria meningitis). 6) Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency).
questions.beyond_mandell: Antibacterial/antifungal pairings draw on general ID pharmacology/guidance rather than this antiviral chapter; only the CMV/herpesvirus activity claims are grounded in Mandell Ch. 46.

cohort_answer.text:
Acyclovir over valacyclovir: HSV meningitis/encephalitis.
Valganciclovir over valacyclovir: Herpes B treatment better activity, CMV treatment.
Famciclovir over acyclovir: Uncomplicated zoster (famciclovir higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir, dosed TID rather than 5 times daily).
Atovaquone over dapsone: G6PD deficiency, Toxoplasmosis.
Doxycycline over TMP-SMX: Someone on Ramipril and Spironolactone with MRSA infection may want Doxycycline over TMP/SMX given risk of hyperkalemia.
Fluconazole over caspofungin: Cryptococcus not covered by echinocandins, urinary or CNS infections.
Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate: CNS infections, disseminated histoplasmosis, suspected mucormycosis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem: Enterococcus.
Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin: Anaerobic activity is best with moxi.
Metronidazole over clindamycin: Bacteroides fragilis, increasing clinda resistance.
Azithromycin over clarithromycin: Better for gram-negatives, esp. M catarrhalis and H flu.
Ampicillin over cloxacillin: Enterococci, Listeria.
Cefazolin over cloxacillin: Surgical prophylaxis, penicillin allergy, AIN, heart failure.

questions.question: An Aeromonas hydrophila isolate has the following susceptibilities: ampicillin (R), ceftriaxone (R), aztreonam (R), meropenem (R), ertapenem (R), tigecycline (S).
questions.question_raw: Q61 (2018). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Aeromonas hydrophila organism with the following susceptibilities: Ampicillin (R), Ceftriaxone (R), Aztreonam (R), Meropenem (R), Ertapenem (R), Tigecycline (S)

parts.text: The organism possesses a carbapenemase that was inactivated by EDTA. Which class of carbapenemase is represented here?
Name one other gram-negative organism found in this same class of beta-lactamases.
Name two other (non-carbapenemase) mechanisms that can cause carbapenem resistance.

parts_raw.text: a) The organism possesses a carbapenemase which was inactivated by EDTA. Which class of carbapenems is represented here?
b) Name one other gram negative found in this same class of beta-lactamases
c) Name two other mechanisms (non-carbapenemase) that can cause carbapenem resistance?

questions.model_answer:
a) Ambler Class B metallo-beta-lactamase (MBL). EDTA chelates the active-site zinc, so inhibition by EDTA defines a zinc-dependent Class B enzyme; Aeromonas carries chromosomal CphA MBLs and acquired VIM/IMP-family MBLs.
b) Any one of: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (VIM/IMP), Klebsiella pneumoniae (NDM), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (L1), Enterobacter cloacae, Escherichia coli (NDM).
c) (1) Loss or reduction of outer-membrane porins (e.g. OprD), decreasing drug entry. (2) Upregulation of efflux pumps (e.g. MexXY), often combined with an AmpC cephalosporinase or ESBL.
questions.beyond_mandell: The porin-loss and efflux mechanisms in part c are standard resistance concepts (CLSI/review literature); the Aeromonas slice names its MBLs but not these non-carbapenemase pathways.

cohort_answer.text: Ambler Class B: MBL. Other GNB in this class: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (also E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacter cloacae). Other mechanisms: decrease or loss of porin (OprD) and increased efflux pump (MexXY)

questions.question: Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to imipenem and meropenem.

parts.text: Name two mechanisms of resistance.

parts_raw.text: Name two mechanisms of Pseudomonas resistance to IMI and MP?

questions.model_answer: (1) Loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (mutational), the principal cause of imipenem resistance and a contributor to meropenem resistance. (2) A carbapenemase — metallo-β-lactamase (VIM, IMP, NDM) or KPC — and/or upregulation of the MexAB-OprM efflux system (which removes meropenem but not imipenem); overexpressed AmpC can also contribute.

cohort_answer.text: MBL, carbapenemase; KPC, porins, efflux pump. Mutational loss of OprD porin, conferring resistance to imipenem; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM). Upregulation of the MexXY efflux system (a member of the RND family), which exports fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, aminoglycosides, and antipseudomonal β-lactam agents. Overexpression of AmpC chromosomal β-lactamases conferring resistance to multiple β-lactam antibiotics

questions.question: An Escherichia coli isolate is resistant to essentially all beta-lactams. Explain the mechanism of beta-lactam resistance, how to test for it, and a risk factor for acquiring it.
questions.question_raw: E. coli resistant to everything mechanism of beta lactam R. How to test for it and risk factor for acquiring?

parts.text: Explain the mechanism of beta-lactam resistance, how to test for it, and a risk factor for acquiring it.

parts_raw.text: E. coli resistant to everything mechanism of beta lactam R. How to test for it and risk factor for acquiring?

questions.model_answer: Mechanism: carbapenemase/beta-lactamase production - e.g. a metallo-beta-lactamase (NDM), OXA-48-type, or plasmid-mediated AmpC (blaCMY-2); ESBL production accounts for cephalosporin resistance. Testing: phenotypic confirmation with the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM/eCIM) or Carba NP, inhibitor-based synergy tests, and molecular PCR for carbapenemase genes (blaNDM, blaKPC, blaOXA-48, blaVIM/IMP). Risk factors: prior broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, healthcare/ICU contact, travel to endemic regions (e.g. NDM in South Asia), and animal/food exposure (poultry, livestock carrying blaCMY-2).
questions.beyond_mandell: Mechanism, mCIM/PCR testing, and epidemiologic risk factors are from CLSI/IDSA resistance guidance (Mandell Ch. 18); not covered in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: ?beta-lactamase production (bla cmy-2; NDM, OXA). Risk factors for acquisition include exposure to animals (poultry, livestock)

questions.question: For each of the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: an Enterobacter species; a Pseudomonas resistant to imipenem/meropenem but susceptible to ceftazidime; a gram-negative bacillus resistant to meropenem but with an increased zone of inhibition when meropenem is combined with EDTA; an Escherichia coli resistant to cephalothin but susceptible to cefazolin.

parts.text: For each of the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: Enterobacter; Pseudomonas resistant to imipenem/meropenem but susceptible to ceftazidime; a gram-negative bacillus resistant to meropenem but with an increased zone with meropenem plus EDTA; Escherichia coli resistant to cephalothin but susceptible to cefazolin.

parts_raw.text: For the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: Enterobacter; Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz; GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero + EDTA; E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin

questions.model_answer: (1) Enterobacter: inducible (or stably derepressed) chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase. (2) Pseudomonas R to imipenem/meropenem but S to ceftazidime: loss of the OprD porin plus efflux-pump upregulation (not carbapenemase-mediated). (3) GNB R to meropenem with larger zone on adding EDTA: metallo-beta-lactamase (EDTA chelates the active-site zinc, restoring activity). (4) E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin: a breakpoint/surrogate artefact - cephalothin is not a reliable predictor of susceptibility to cefazolin and other cephalosporins.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Enterobacter AmpC mechanism is in this chapter; porin/efflux, MBL-EDTA synergy, and the cephalothin surrogate issue are from CLSI resistance guidance (Mandell Ch. 18).

cohort_answer.text: Enterobacter - AmpC. Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz - Porin mediated and efflux pump. GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero+EDTA - Metallo beta lactamase. E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin - cephalothin breakpoints do not reliably predict susceptibilities of cephalexin and other cephalosporins.

parts.text: What are the two other most common/clinically relevant carbapenemases?
What are two recommended treatments per IDSA guidelines?

parts_raw.text: What are the two other most common/clinically relevant carbapenemases?
What are two recommended treatments per IDSA guidelines

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) KPC (Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase, class A) and (2) OXA-48-type (class D). (NDM is the leading class B metallo-beta-lactamase.)
b) For NDM-producing Enterobacterales, IDSA recommends either (1) cefiderocol, or (2) ceftazidime-avibactam PLUS aztreonam (or aztreonam-avibactam where available).
questions.beyond_mandell: Carbapenemase classification and NDM treatment options are from the IDSA guidance on AMR gram-negative infections; not covered in this chapter.
